uuidTool.title: UUID Generator
uuidTool.privacy: UUIDs are generated in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server.
uuidTool.constantHint: This value is defined by the RFC and never changes.

hints.v1: Timestamp plus node. Useful for time-aware IDs, not for privacy.
hints.v3: Name-based with MD5. The same name always produces the same UUID.
hints.v4: Random 122-bit IDs. The default choice for most apps.
hints.v5: Name-based with SHA-1. Prefer this over v3 for deterministic IDs.
hints.v6: Reordered v1 timestamp so values sort in time order.
hints.v7: Unix time-ordered. The best UUID for database primary keys.
hints.v8: Custom layout filled with a cryptographically secure random source.
hints.nil: All zeros. A sentinel empty value.
hints.max: All ones. A sentinel maximum value.

count.label: How many
count.lockedHelper: Name-based and constant UUIDs always generate one value.

nameBased.title: Name and namespace
nameBased.helper: The same name and namespace always produce the same UUID.
nameBased.name: Name
nameBased.nameHelper: A domain, URL, or any string to hash.

inspector.title: Decode
inspector.invalid: That is not a valid UUID.
inspector.empty: Generate a UUID to inspect it.

v1.body: A version 1 UUID encodes a Gregorian timestamp, a clock sequence, and a 48-bit node. In the browser the node is a random value with the multicast bit set, not a hardware MAC address.
v1.use: Legacy systems that already expect v1, or cases where you need a timestamp plus a stable node for the session.
v1.avoid: Public IDs. The timestamp (and a node) can leak when the value was created.

v3.body: A version 3 UUID is a 128-bit MD5 hash of a namespace UUID plus a name. It is deterministic: the same inputs always yield the same output.
v3.use: Stable IDs derived from a name when you must match an existing MD5-based system.
v3.avoid: New designs. Prefer v5 (SHA-1) for name-based IDs, or v4/v7 for unique keys.

v4.body: A version 4 UUID is made almost entirely of random data: 122 of 128 bits are random, and the rest record the version and variant. This generator uses a cryptographically secure source.
v4.use: General-purpose IDs for APIs, files, request tracing, and anything that must not reveal when it was created.
v4.avoid: Large indexed database tables where insert locality matters. Prefer v7 there.

v5.body: A version 5 UUID hashes a namespace and name with SHA-1, then sets the version and variant bits. Like v3, it is deterministic.
v5.use: IDs that must be reproducible from a URL, domain, or other unique name.
v5.avoid: Secrets. A name-based UUID is guessable if the name is guessable.

v6.body: Version 6 keeps the v1 timestamp and node, but reorders the bits so the most significant time bits come first. Values sort in creation order.
v6.use: A time-ordered drop-in when you already have v1 data and need lexicographic sort.
v6.avoid: New databases. v7 is simpler and uses Unix time in milliseconds.

v7.body: A version 7 UUID stores a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, then random bits. Later values sort after earlier ones, which keeps B-tree indexes healthy.
v7.use: Primary keys, event IDs, and any store that is scanned in time order.
v7.avoid: IDs that must hide creation time. Use v4 when the timestamp would be a leak.

v8.body: Version 8 is the RFC 9562 custom layout. This tool fills it with a cryptographically secure random source and sets the version and variant bits.
v8.use: Experiments and custom schemes that need the v8 version nibble.
v8.avoid: Standard application IDs. Prefer v4 or v7 unless you have a defined custom layout.

nil.body: The nil UUID is 128 zero bits. RFC 9562 defines it as a sentinel for “no value”.
nil.use: Placeholder or missing-value representation in APIs and databases.
nil.avoid: Using it as a real identifier. Every nil UUID is the same.

max.body: The max UUID is 128 one bits. RFC 9562 defines it as the maximum sentinel value.
max.use: Range queries, exclusive upper bounds, or a defined “greater than any UUID” token.
max.avoid: Using it as a unique key. Every max UUID is the same.
